items.topic: Regulations governing practice before the IRS (Circular 230)
items.task: Apply a practitioner's duties, restrictions and standards under Circular 230 to a scenario.
items.task_source: author-drafted from Blueprint topic name (지도.json has no Group A/B/D)
items.stem: Nadia Ferro, CPA, is drafting a written opinion for Brightline Lodging LLC on whether the investors in its new hotel will be able to deduct the LLC's early-year losses. The exhibit lists four statements from the draft letter. Which statement would make the letter inconsistent with the standards for written tax advice if it stays in the final letter?
exhibit: We assumed that construction will be finished by October 2026, because the loan agreement we reviewed requires completion by that date.
We related the loss-limitation rules and the authorities we cite to the facts described in this letter and explained our reasoning.
We accepted the promoter's projection of 95% occupancy without testing it, although our own workpapers show comparable hotels in the market averaging about 60%.
We relied on the manager's written statement that the LLC has no debt other than the bank loan; nothing in the records we saw contradicts it.
options: Statement 1, the assumption about the completion date
Statement 2, the application of the loss rules to the stated facts
Statement 3, the acceptance of the occupancy projection
Statement 4, the reliance on the manager's statement about debt

why.A: A reasonable assumption about a future event, supported by a document the practitioner reviewed and disclosed in the letter, is allowed.
why.B: Relating the law and authorities to the facts is required in written advice, so this statement supports the letter.
why.C: Written advice may not rely on a projection when the reliance is unreasonable. Nadia's own workpapers contradict the 95% figure, so she ignored facts she knows and relied unreasonably on the promoter.
why.D: Reasonable reliance on a written statement from the client's manager is allowed when nothing in the file contradicts it.

items.rule_line: Written tax advice may not rely on projections or assumptions that are unreasonable given facts the practitioner knows.

guide.ask: May written advice rely on a projection or an assumption?
guide.reveal: Only if the reliance is reasonable and the practitioner does not ignore facts he knows.

guide.ask: Which draft statement conflicts with the workpapers showing about 60% occupancy?
guide.reveal: The acceptance of the promoter's 95% projection without testing it.

items.topic: Regulations governing practice before the IRS (Circular 230)
items.task: Apply a practitioner's duties, restrictions and standards under Circular 230 to a scenario.
items.task_source: author-drafted from Blueprint topic name (지도.json has no Group A/B/D)
items.stem: Which situation presents a conflict of interest for Imani Okafor, CPA, that she may accept only if she reasonably believes she can serve every client competently and diligently and each affected client gives informed consent that is confirmed in writing?
options: She represents two competing restaurants, each in a separate IRS examination that raises unrelated issues.
She represents a husband in an examination of a joint return and his wife in a request for relief from liability on that return.
She represents a client in the examination of a return she prepared, and the IRS has raised no question about her work.
She represents a corporation in an IRS matter and earlier prepared returns for its former owner in an unrelated engagement that has ended.

why.A: Business rivalry does not make the clients' positions before the IRS directly adverse, and nothing limits her work for either client, so no conflict arises.
why.B: Relief for the wife would shift liability to the husband, so representing both is directly adverse. Imani may proceed only with each client's informed consent, confirmed in writing, and a reasonable belief that she can serve both competently and diligently.
why.C: A personal-interest conflict needs a significant risk that her own interest would materially limit the representation, such as a preparer penalty proposed against her. Nothing here suggests that.
why.D: A duty to a former client creates a conflict only if it materially limits the current representation. The earlier engagement is unrelated and finished.

items.rule_line: Directly adverse client interests, such as spouses in innocent-spouse relief, need reasonable belief and informed written consent; mere business rivalry is not adversity.

guide.ask: When are two clients directly adverse in a conflict of interest?
guide.reveal: When helping one shifts liability or advantage away from the other.

guide.ask: In which pairing does relief for the wife shift liability to the husband on the same return?
guide.reveal: The joint-return examination for the husband alongside the wife's relief request; the firm needs each client's informed written consent and a reasonable belief it can serve both.

items.topic: Regulations governing practice before the IRS (Circular 230)
items.task: Apply a practitioner's duties, restrictions and standards under Circular 230 to a scenario.
items.task_source: author-drafted from Blueprint topic name (지도.json has no Group A/B/D)
items.stem: Ravi Menon, EA, is asked to quote fees for IRS work. Under Circular 230, which arrangement is a contingent fee?
options: An hourly rate of $250, billed monthly for all of the time Ravi spends on the client's examination
A fee of 1% of the client's gross receipts, charged for monthly bookkeeping that is unrelated to any tax position
A fixed fee of $4,000 set in advance, payable half at signing and half on delivery of the completed return
A fixed fee of $4,000 for a return, refunded to the client if the IRS later disallows a position on it

why.A: Time-based billing does not depend on the outcome of any position, so it is not a contingent fee.
why.B: A percentage fee is contingent only when it turns on whether a tax position is sustained or on a tax result. This fee depends on receipts for bookkeeping, not on a tax result.
why.C: A fee fixed in advance and payable on stated dates is not tied to any result, so it is not contingent.
why.D: A fee that is returned if a return position is not sustained depends on the result. Circular 230 treats reimbursement guarantees like this as contingent fees even though the stated fee is fixed.

items.rule_line: Under Circular 230 a fee that depends on the outcome, including one refundable if a position fails, is contingent.

guide.ask: What makes a fee contingent under Circular 230?
guide.reveal: Its amount depends on the result, including a fee that is refunded if a position is not sustained.

guide.ask: Which arrangement is fixed at $4,000 yet reimbursed if the IRS disallows the position?
guide.reveal: That one, because the reimbursement guarantee ties the fee to the outcome.

items.topic: Regulations governing practice before the IRS (Circular 230)
items.task: Apply a practitioner's duties, restrictions and standards under Circular 230 to a scenario.
items.task_source: author-drafted from Blueprint topic name (지도.json has no Group A/B/D)
items.stem: During an examination of a client's 2024 return, a revenue agent makes a proper written request to Jorge Ibarra, CPA, for the client's 2024 payroll records. Neither Jorge nor the client has the records. The client says that a former payroll company holds them and refuses to release them to the client. What must Jorge do under Circular 230?
options: Ask the client who holds the records, then promptly tell the agent that neither has them and name the company as the client reports
Say nothing more, because the IRS can summon the payroll company itself and Jorge has no duty to say who might hold the records
Contact the payroll company himself, confirm exactly what records it holds, and deliver copies of them to the revenue agent
Tell the agent that the records are privileged, because they were created for the client's business and not for use by the IRS

why.A: When records are outside the control of both practitioner and client, the practitioner must promptly notify the IRS and give the identity of the holder as the client reports it, after reasonable inquiry of the client.
why.B: The practitioner must promptly notify the IRS and share what he knows about who holds the records. The IRS's ability to issue a summons does not remove that duty.
why.C: The practitioner need only ask his client and pass on the answer. He is not required to make inquiry of anyone else or to verify what the client says.
why.D: The privilege exception applies only if the practitioner believes in good faith and on reasonable grounds that the records are privileged. Ordinary business records held by a third party are not.

items.rule_line: If records are held by neither practitioner nor client, the practitioner must promptly notify the IRS and identify the holder as the client reports.

guide.ask: Are the records within the control of Jorge or the client?
guide.reveal: No, a former payroll company holds them and will not release them to the client.

guide.ask: What must the practitioner do after reasonable inquiry of the client?
guide.reveal: Promptly tell the agent that neither has the records and name the holder as the client reports.

items.topic: Regulations governing practice before the IRS (Circular 230)
items.task: Apply a practitioner's duties, restrictions and standards under Circular 230 to a scenario.
items.task_source: author-drafted from Blueprint topic name (지도.json has no Group A/B/D)
items.stem: In 2026, Carlos Vega, CPA, is preparing a client's 2025 return. He finds that the 2024 return he prepared reported a $200,000 net operating loss when the supportable loss is $50,000, because personal expenses were deducted. Carlos has explained the error and its consequences to the client, who refuses to amend the 2024 return and insists that the 2025 return use the full $200,000 loss carryover. What is Carlos's position under Circular 230?
options: He must report the 2024 error to the IRS before he may prepare any 2025 return for the client
He may sign the 2025 return with the full carryover, because once he advised the client his duty for the 2024 error ended
He must file an amended 2024 return himself, because he prepared it and his duty of care runs to the IRS
He need not notify the IRS, but he may not sign a 2025 return that claims a carryover he knows is unsupported

why.A: Circular 230 requires advising the client, not reporting to the IRS, and client confidentiality restricts disclosure.
why.B: Advising the client satisfies only the duty for the prior return. Carrying the known error into a new return means signing a position he knows is unsupported.
why.C: A practitioner cannot amend a client's return on his own, and Circular 230 does not require him to do so.
why.D: The duty for a known prior-year error is to advise the client of the error and its consequences; there is no duty to notify the IRS or to amend. But a practitioner may not sign a return containing a position he knows lacks a reasonable basis.

items.rule_line: A practitioner who knows of a prior-year error must advise the client, need not tell the IRS, but may not sign a return carrying the unsupported position.

guide.ask: What is the duty for a known prior-year error?
guide.reveal: Advise the client of the error and its consequences; there is no duty to notify the IRS or amend.

guide.ask: May Carlos sign a 2025 return that claims a carryover he knows is unsupported?
guide.reveal: No, a practitioner may not sign a position lacking a reasonable basis.

items.topic: Internal Revenue Code and regulations related to tax return preparers
items.task: Identify penalties, requirements and prohibitions that apply to tax return preparers.
items.task_source: author-drafted from Blueprint topic name (지도.json has no Group A/B/D)
items.stem: Lena and Tomas each prepared a client's return claiming the same $70,000 deduction, as shown in the exhibit. Neither return involves a tax shelter or reportable transaction, neither preparer acted willfully or recklessly, and the IRS disallows both deductions. Which statement about the preparer penalty for an unreasonable position is correct?
exhibit: $70,000 deduction; reasonable basis but no substantial authority
options: Only Tomas is subject to the penalty, because disclosing a reasonable-basis position protects the preparer
Neither preparer is subject to the penalty, because the position had a reasonable basis in both of the returns
Both preparers are subject to the penalty, because the position lacked substantial authority in both of the returns
Only Lena is subject to the penalty, because her disclosure shows that she knew the position was weak when she filed

why.A: A preparer is not penalized for a position that has a reasonable basis and is adequately disclosed. Lena disclosed. Tomas took the same position without substantial authority or disclosure and has no reasonable cause.
why.B: A reasonable basis protects a preparer only when the position is also adequately disclosed. Tomas did not disclose, so it does not protect him.
why.C: Lack of substantial authority is enough only for an undisclosed position. Lena's disclosure of a position with a reasonable basis avoids the penalty.
why.D: Disclosure is not evidence of wrongdoing. It is the step that protects a preparer whose position has a reasonable basis.

items.rule_line: A reasonable-basis position avoids the preparer penalty only if adequately disclosed; otherwise substantial authority is needed.

guide.ask: Which positions escape the preparer penalty?
guide.reveal: Those with substantial authority, or with a reasonable basis and adequate disclosure.

guide.ask: Which preparer disclosed and which did not, given the same reasonable-basis position?
guide.reveal: Lena disclosed, so she is protected; Tomas did not disclose and had no reasonable cause, so he is exposed.

items.topic: AICPA Statements on Standards for Tax Services and Code of Professional Conduct
items.task: Apply the AICPA tax practice standards and Code provisions to a scenario.
items.task_source: author-drafted from Blueprint topic name (지도.json has no Group A/B/D)
items.stem: Halden & Pryor, CPAs, audit the financial statements of Kestrel Products Inc. and also provide tax services to Kestrel. Which tax service would impair the firm's independence for the audit under the AICPA Code of Professional Conduct?
options: Preparing Kestrel's federal return from records its staff assembled, after which its chief financial officer reviews, approves and signs it
Deciding for Kestrel, without its approval, which of two supportable positions its return will take and directing the staff to file it
Advising Kestrel on the federal tax effects of a proposed acquisition while its board decides whether to proceed
Preparing an amended return for Kestrel for a flat fee agreed in advance and not tied to any refund

why.A: Return preparation does not impair independence when management makes the decisions and takes responsibility for the return, as it does here.
why.B: Making decisions that belong to management is assuming a management responsibility, which impairs independence for an attest client.
why.C: Tax planning advice is allowed when management makes the decision, and here the board makes it.
why.D: A contingent fee for preparing an amended return would violate the Contingent Fees Rule. This fee is fixed and not tied to any result, so the service is permitted.

cite.ref: Code 1.295.160.03 (tax services) and 1.295.040.01 (general requirements for nonattest services)

items.law_note: AICPA revised Tax Services interpretation (1.295.160) effective 2026-12-31 (early adoption permitted); the answer is the same under both versions.
items.rule_line: Making decisions that belong to management for an attest client impairs independence; return preparation with management approval does not.

guide.ask: What kind of act by a tax adviser impairs independence for an audit client?
guide.reveal: Assuming a management responsibility.

guide.ask: Which listed service has the firm making a decision that belongs to management without its approval?
guide.reveal: Deciding which return position Kestrel will take and directing staff to file it.

items.topic: AICPA Statements on Standards for Tax Services and Code of Professional Conduct
items.task: Apply the AICPA tax practice standards and Code provisions to a scenario.
items.task_source: author-drafted from Blueprint topic name (지도.json has no Group A/B/D)
items.stem: Which disclosure of confidential client information by a CPA in public practice would violate the AICPA Code of Professional Conduct because it is made without the client's specific consent?
options: Answering a written inquiry from the state board of accountancy that is investigating a complaint about the CPA's work for the client
Giving client files to a reviewer who is performing a peer review of the CPA's practice under an authorized review program
Telling a banker friend, who asked informally about the client's creditworthiness, that the client's profits fell last year
Complying with a validly issued and enforceable subpoena from a court in a civil suit against the client

why.A: The Code allows a member to respond to inquiries from a duly constituted investigative or disciplinary body without client consent.
why.B: Review of a member's practice under an authorized program is an exception, and the reviewer must keep the information confidential.
why.C: Disclosing confidential client information to a third party for that party's use requires the client's specific consent. No exception covers an informal answer to a bank contact.
why.D: A valid, enforceable subpoena is an exception, so compliance does not violate the confidentiality rule.

items.rule_line: A CPA may disclose confidential client information without consent to a board inquiry, peer review or enforceable subpoena, not to an informal third-party inquiry.

guide.ask: When may a CPA disclose confidential client information without specific consent?
guide.reveal: For legal process, licensing or disciplinary inquiries, and peer review.

guide.ask: Which of the listed disclosures fits none of these?
guide.reveal: The informal answer to a banker friend about the client's creditworthiness.

items.topic: Licensing and disciplinary systems
items.task: Identify sanctions, eligibility rules and disciplinary procedures for practitioners.
items.task_source: author-drafted from Blueprint topic name (지도.json has no Group A/B/D)
items.stem: The IRS finds that Marcus Hale, a CPA employed by Dunmore & Lyle, prepared documents for an IRS matter that willfully misstated facts, and that the firm earned $30,000 in fees for the work. The Secretary of the Treasury proceeds against Marcus. Which statement about a monetary penalty on the firm itself is correct?
options: The firm may be fined up to $30,000, its fees, if it knew or reasonably should have known of Marcus's conduct
The firm may be fined up to $30,000 in every case, because it profited from the fees earned on the work
The firm cannot be fined, because a monetary penalty may be imposed only on the individual practitioner who acted
The firm may be fined up to $60,000, twice its fees, if it knew of Marcus's conduct and profited from it

why.A: The Secretary may impose a monetary penalty on an employer or firm if it knew or reasonably should have known of the conduct. The penalty is capped at the gross income derived from the conduct, here $30,000.
why.B: Earning the fees is not enough. The firm must have known, or reasonably should have known, of the conduct.
why.C: The rules expressly allow a penalty on the employer, firm or entity on whose behalf the practitioner acted.
why.D: The cap is the gross income derived or to be derived from the conduct, not a multiple of it.

items.rule_line: A firm may be fined up to the gross income from the conduct if it knew or reasonably should have known of the practitioner's conduct.

guide.ask: May a monetary penalty be imposed on the firm?
guide.reveal: Yes, if the firm knew or reasonably should have known of the conduct.

guide.ask: What caps it?
guide.reveal: The gross income derived from the conduct, here $30,000.

items.topic: Licensing and disciplinary systems
items.task: Identify sanctions, eligibility rules and disciplinary procedures for practitioners.
items.task_source: author-drafted from Blueprint topic name (지도.json has no Group A/B/D)
items.stem: The IRS establishes that Priya Nair, a CPA, willfully understated the tax on 40 client returns she prepared. Her state board of accountancy has already suspended her license for one year for the same conduct. Which statement is correct?
options: The IRS must wait until the suspension ends, because only one authority may discipline the same practitioner at a time
The IRS is barred from any further action over the same conduct, because a second penalty would be double jeopardy
The IRS may act only by asking the state board to lengthen the suspension, because states have exclusive power over CPAs
The IRS may still assess preparer penalties and seek sanctions, and the state action may itself support discipline

why.A: Each authority acts under its own rules and no single-forum rule exists, so the IRS need not wait for the state board.
why.B: Administrative and civil penalties and sanctions by different authorities are separate proceedings. The state action does not bar them.
why.C: The IRS regulates practice before the IRS and enforces preparer penalties. The state's licensing power is not exclusive.
why.D: The proceedings are independent. The IRS can pursue its own preparer penalties and sanctions, and a state suspension is itself conduct that can support IRS discipline.

items.rule_line: State board discipline does not bar independent IRS preparer penalties and Circular 230 sanctions for the same conduct.

guide.ask: Are IRS and state licensing discipline independent?
guide.reveal: Yes, each authority may act separately.

guide.ask: What does the state suspension mean for the IRS?
guide.reveal: The IRS may still assess preparer penalties and seek sanctions, and the state action can itself support discipline.

items.topic: Audits, appeals and the judicial process
items.task: Explain the audit and appeals process as it relates to tax matters.
items.task_source: 지도.json
items.stem: Hannah Doyle timely filed her 2023 individual return, which reported gross income of $200,000. It left out $30,000 of income that she overlooked. The IRS has not begun an examination, and Hannah has not signed any agreement extending the assessment period. Which change in the facts would give the IRS an unlimited period to assess additional tax for 2023?
options: The omitted income turns out to be $60,000, which is more than 25% of the gross income stated on the return
Hannah left out the income on purpose, and the IRS proves she filed a false return intending to evade tax
Hannah filed the return on October 15, 2024 under a valid extension, rather than in March as she did
Hannah files an amended return that reports the omitted income and pays the additional tax with interest

why.A: Omitting more than 25% of the gross income stated on the return extends the period to six years, not to an unlimited period.
why.B: A false or fraudulent return filed with intent to evade tax leaves the assessment period open indefinitely.
why.C: A return filed under extension is still subject to the three-year period, which then runs from the later filing date.
why.D: An amended return does not create an unlimited period. Reporting the income voluntarily does not extend the general three-year period.

items.rule_line: Unlimited assessment time applies to fraud or unfiled returns; omitting over 25% of gross income gives six years.

guide.ask: Which circumstance leaves the assessment period open indefinitely?
guide.reveal: A false or fraudulent return filed with intent to evade tax.

guide.ask: Do a 25% omission, an extension or an amended return do that?
guide.reveal: No, they only lengthen or leave the period unchanged, so the intent-to-evade fact is decisive.

items.topic: Substantiation and disclosure
items.task: Identify whether substantiation is sufficient given a specific scenario.
items.task_source: 지도.json
items.stem: Ruth Alvarez, a self-employed consultant, kept no receipts, logs or other records of her 2025 business expenses. On examining her 2025 return, the IRS disallows all of her business deductions for lack of documentation. For which expense could a court still allow a reasonable estimate, if Ruth shows she incurred the expense and gives a reasonable basis for the amount?
options: Airfare and hotel for a client meeting in another city
The business share of her car's use, for which she kept no log
Office supplies bought for use in the consulting business
A holiday gift she gave to an important client

why.A: Travel expenses must meet the strict substantiation rules, so a court may not estimate them.
why.B: Listed property such as a vehicle is subject to the strict substantiation rules, and an estimate is not enough.
why.C: Expenses outside the strict rules for travel, gifts and listed property may be estimated under the Cohan rule when the taxpayer shows the expense was incurred and gives a reasonable basis for the amount. (Lost records from a casualty such as a flood could instead be reasonably reconstructed under Treas. Reg. §1.274-5T(c)(5); here no records were ever kept.)
why.D: Gifts are subject to the strict substantiation rules, so the court may not estimate the amount.

items.rule_line: Cohan estimates are allowed for expenses outside the strict substantiation rules for travel, gifts and listed property.

guide.ask: Which expenses may not be estimated when records are missing?
guide.reveal: Travel, gifts and listed property, which face strict substantiation.

guide.ask: Which listed expense falls outside those rules and can be estimated under Cohan?
guide.reveal: Office supplies used in the consulting business.

items.topic: Audits, appeals and the judicial process
items.task: Explain the audit and appeals process as it relates to tax matters.
items.task_source: 지도.json
items.stem: Renee Baptiste filed her 2023 individual return on February 12, 2024. The return was due April 15, 2024, and she did not extend it. All of her tax for 2023 was paid through withholding. In September 2026 she finds an overlooked deduction that would produce a refund. What is the last day on which she can file a timely claim for refund?
options: April 15, 2026
February 12, 2027
April 15, 2027
October 15, 2027

why.A: Counts two years from the day withholding is treated as paid. The claim period is the later of that date and three years from filing, so the two-year date is too early.
why.B: Counts three years from the actual early filing date. A return filed before its due date is treated as filed on the due date.
why.C: The early return is treated as filed on April 15, 2024, and withholding is treated as paid the same day. The later of three years from filing and two years from payment is April 15, 2027.
why.D: Adds a six-month extension to the three years. Renee did not extend the return, so no extra time applies.

steps: A return filed early is treated as filed on the due date, April 15, 2024
Withholding is treated as paid on April 15, 2024
Claim period is the later of 3 years from filing or 2 years from payment: 3 years from April 15, 2024
items.rule_line: A refund claim is due by the later of three years from filing (early returns count as filed on the due date) or two years from payment.

guide.ask: How are an early return and withholding treated for the refund claim period?
guide.reveal: Both are treated as filed and paid on the due date, April 15, 2024.

guide.ask: What is the claim period?
guide.reveal: The later of 3 years from filing or 2 years from payment, so 3 years.

guide.ask: What date is 3 years after April 15, 2024?

items.topic: Audits, appeals and the judicial process
items.task: Explain the different levels of the judicial process as they relate to tax matters.
items.task_source: 지도.json
items.stem: The exhibit shows a notice of deficiency mailed to Kenji Arai. Kenji wants to petition the Tax Court. What is the last day on which a petition is timely?
options: January 5, 2027
March 5, 2027
March 6, 2027
March 8, 2027

why.A: Uses 90 days, which applies to a notice addressed to a person in the United States.
why.B: Moves back to the previous business day. A deadline that falls on a weekend moves forward to the next business day.
why.C: Correctly counts 150 days but ignores that March 6, 2027 is a Saturday.
why.D: A notice addressed to a person outside the United States allows 150 days. 150 days after October 7, 2026 is Saturday, March 6, 2027, so the deadline moves to Monday, March 8, 2027.

steps: Notice is addressed to a person outside the United States, so the period is 150 days
A deadline on a Saturday, Sunday or legal holiday moves to the next business day: Monday, March 8, 2027
items.rule_line: A notice of deficiency mailed outside the U.S. allows 150 days, and a weekend deadline moves to the next business day.

guide.ask: How long does a taxpayer with a notice addressed outside the United States have?
guide.reveal: 150 days.

guide.ask: What is October 7, 2026 plus 150 days?
guide.reveal: Saturday, March 6, 2027.

guide.ask: What happens when the deadline falls on a Saturday?
guide.reveal: It moves to the next business day, Monday, March 8, 2027.

items.topic: Audits, appeals and the judicial process
items.task: Explain the different levels of the judicial process as they relate to tax matters.
items.task_source: 지도.json
items.stem: The IRS mailed Elena Kowalczyk notices of deficiency for 2023 and 2024 showing the amounts in the exhibit. Elena disputes every amount. For which year or years may she ask the Tax Court to use its small tax case procedure?
options: Both years, because each year's deficiency by itself is $50,000 or less
Neither year, because the two years together exceed $50,000
Neither year, because the small tax case procedure is not available when a penalty is asserted
2024 only, because the deficiency and penalty in dispute for that year total $50,000 or less

why.A: The amount in dispute includes penalties. Adding the $8,800 penalty puts 2023 above $50,000.
why.B: The limit is applied separately to each taxable year, not to the total of all years in the case.
why.C: Penalties may be part of a small tax case. They simply count toward the limit.
why.D: The limit applies to each tax year and counts penalties. 2024 totals $25,200, which qualifies, but 2023 totals $52,800, which does not.

items.law_note: The $50,000 small tax case limit is a fixed statutory amount, not inflation adjusted.
items.rule_line: The small tax case limit is $50,000 per tax year including penalties, applied separately to each year.

guide.ask: Does the small tax case limit apply per year, and does it count penalties?
guide.reveal: Yes to both.

guide.ask: What are the year totals against the limit?
guide.reveal: 2023 totals 52,800, which exceeds 50,000, and 2024 totals 25,200, which does not; only the lower year qualifies.

items.topic: Audits, appeals and the judicial process
items.task: Explain the different levels of the judicial process as they relate to tax matters.
items.task_source: 지도.json
items.stem: Paolo Ricci received a notice of deficiency for 2023 showing a $52,000 deficiency. He did not petition the Tax Court within the time allowed, and the IRS assessed the tax. Paolo now believes the IRS was wrong on the merits. Which route to judicial review is still open to him?
options: Pay the tax, file a timely refund claim, and sue for a refund in a district court or the Court of Federal Claims if it is denied
File a late petition in the Tax Court, which the court may accept for up to one year after the tax is assessed
Ask the Independent Office of Appeals to reopen the year, with its decision then reviewable in the Tax Court on petition
Sue in a district court to stop collection without paying first, because he disputes the assessment on the merits

why.A: After the Tax Court route is lost, the remaining route is to pay in full, file a timely refund claim, and sue for a refund in a district court or the Court of Federal Claims.
why.B: No general one-year grace period exists for a Tax Court petition after a notice of deficiency.
why.C: Appeals has no procedure that revives the Tax Court's review of an assessed deficiency.
why.D: A suit to restrain assessment or collection is generally barred, and a refund suit requires full payment first.

items.rule_line: After missing the Tax Court deadline, review requires paying in full, filing a refund claim and suing in district court or the Court of Federal Claims.

guide.ask: Has Paolo lost the prepayment Tax Court route?
guide.reveal: Yes, the petition deadline passed and the tax was assessed.

guide.ask: What judicial route remains?
guide.reveal: Pay the tax in full, file a timely refund claim, and sue for refund in a district court or the Court of Federal Claims.

items.topic: Audits, appeals and the judicial process
items.task: Explain the audit and appeals process as it relates to tax matters.
items.task_source: 지도.json
items.stem: After an examination, the IRS offers Ilse Brandt two ways to settle her 2023 tax year: signing Form 870, a waiver of restrictions on assessment, or entering into a closing agreement on Form 866. Which statement correctly compares the two?
options: Both are closing agreements, so neither the IRS nor Ilse may reopen 2023 except for fraud, malfeasance or misrepresentation
Form 870 permits assessment now and does not bar a refund claim, while Form 866 is final except for fraud or misrepresentation
Form 870 is a final closing agreement, while Form 866 lets Ilse pay and claim a refund for 2023 later if she disagrees
Form 866 only waives the restrictions on assessment, and Form 870 also settles every later year that raises the same issue

why.A: Only the closing agreement has that finality. Form 870 is a waiver of restrictions on assessment and is not a closing agreement.
why.B: Form 870 is not a final closing agreement, so it does not stop Ilse from paying and claiming a refund later. A closing agreement is final and conclusive except for fraud, malfeasance or misrepresentation of a material fact.
why.C: This reverses the two forms. The closing agreement, not the waiver, is the final one.
why.D: Neither form settles later years. The closing agreement is the final agreement for the matters it covers.

cite.ref: Form 870 (Rev. 3-1992), instructions: General Information, Who Must Sign
IRM 8.6.4.6 (Forms 866 and 906 give closing-agreement finality under IRC 7121)

items.rule_line: Form 870 waives restrictions on assessment and permits a refund claim, while a Form 866 closing agreement is final except for fraud or misrepresentation.

guide.ask: Is Form 870 a final closing agreement?
guide.reveal: No, it waives restrictions on assessment so the IRS can assess now, and does not bar a later refund claim.

guide.ask: How final is Form 866?
guide.reveal: It is a closing agreement, final and conclusive except for fraud, malfeasance or misrepresentation of a material fact.

items.stem: Alberto Rojas's return understated his tax. The exhibit summarizes the revenue agent's findings. What total civil penalty applies to the underpayment?
exhibit: Portion the IRS proves is due to fraud
Portion Alberto proves, by a preponderance of the evidence, is not due to fraud (substantial understatement; no defense applies)

why.A: 20% of the whole $120,000. This ignores the fraud penalty that applies to the portion due to fraud.
why.B: 75% of the $80,000 fraud portion only. It omits the 20% accuracy-related penalty on the remaining $40,000.
why.C: The fraud penalty of 75% applies to the $80,000 fraud portion ($60,000). Because Alberto proved the other $40,000 is not fraud, the 20% accuracy-related penalty applies to it ($8,000). Total $68,000.
why.D: 75% of the entire $120,000. That result applies only if Alberto fails to prove that the $40,000 is not due to fraud.

steps: Alberto proves 40,000 is not fraud, so the 20% accuracy-related penalty applies to it: 20% x 40,000 = 8,000
items.rule_line: The fraud penalty is 75% of the fraud portion, and the 20% accuracy penalty applies to the remaining portion shown not fraudulent.

guide.ask: What penalty applies to the $80,000 the IRS proves is fraud?
What applies to the $40,000 Alberto proves is not fraud?
guide.reveal: The 20% accuracy-related penalty: 20% x 40,000 = 8,000.

guide.ask: What is the total?

items.topic: Taxpayer penalties
items.task: Identify taxpayer penalties given a specific scenario.
items.task_source: 지도.json
items.stem: The exhibit summarizes an examination of Sophie Lindqvist's individual return. What accuracy-related penalty applies to the $90,000 underpayment?
exhibit: No reasonable attempt to keep adequate records; no substantial authority; no reasonable cause
Position with a reasonable basis; not a tax shelter
Tax shown $60,000; correct tax $150,000; no fraud

why.A: Item 2 is disclosed with a reasonable basis, so no penalty applies to it. Item 1 is both negligent and a substantial understatement, but penalties do not stack: 20% x $70,000 = $14,000.
why.B: 20% of the full $90,000. It ignores that Item 2 is disclosed with a reasonable basis and is not penalized.
why.C: 40% of $70,000. It adds the negligence and substantial-understatement rates together, but no stacking of rates is allowed.
why.D: 75% of $70,000, the civil fraud rate. Fraud is not asserted.

steps: Item 2 ($20,000) is adequately disclosed and has a reasonable basis: no penalty
Item 1 understatement after reduction: 90,000 - 20,000 = 70,000; threshold = greater of 10% x 150,000 = 15,000 or 5,000 = 15,000; 70,000 > 15,000, so substantial
Negligence and substantial understatement overlap on the same 70,000; the rate does not stack
items.rule_line: Accuracy-related penalties do not stack, and a disclosed item with reasonable basis is not penalized.

guide.ask: Is the $20,000 item penalized, given disclosure and reasonable basis?
guide.reveal: No, adequate disclosure with a reasonable basis removes it.

guide.ask: What is the remaining understatement and does it exceed the threshold?
Do negligence and substantial understatement stack, and what is the penalty?
guide.reveal: No, one 20% rate applies: 20% x 70,000 = 14,000.

items.topic: Taxpayer penalties
items.task: Identify taxpayer penalties given a specific scenario.
items.task_source: 지도.json
items.stem: The IRS disallowed a deduction on each of four unrelated returns and asserted the accuracy-related penalty. Each taxpayer claims reasonable cause based on reliance on someone else. Which taxpayer is most likely to establish reasonable cause and good faith?
options: Vera, who bought an aggressive shelter on the advice of the promoter who sold it and who earned a fee from her investment
Dev, who hired an experienced CPA but described the deduction only as a consulting expense and left out that the payee was his own company
Gwen, who gave an experienced CPA all the relevant facts and took the position the CPA recommended after reviewing the authorities
Owen, who followed the tax advice of his brother-in-law, a bookkeeper with no tax training, because it saved the most tax

why.A: Reliance on a promoter who profits from the transaction is generally not reasonable.
why.B: Reliance fails when the taxpayer withholds facts the adviser needs, so the advice was not based on all the relevant facts.
why.C: Reasonable cause is shown when the adviser is competent, the taxpayer gives the adviser complete and accurate information, and the taxpayer actually relies in good faith. Gwen meets all three.
why.D: The adviser must be competent in tax matters. Reliance on someone without that expertise is not reasonable.

cite.ref: Neonatology Associates, P.A. v. Commissioner, 115 T.C. 43 (2000), aff'd, 299 F.3d 221 (3d Cir. 2002)

items.rule_line: Reasonable cause requires a competent adviser, complete information and good-faith reliance.

guide.ask: What three elements support reasonable cause based on an adviser?
guide.reveal: A competent adviser, complete and accurate information given, and actual good-faith reliance.

guide.ask: Which taxpayer supplied all the facts to an experienced CPA and followed that advice?
guide.reveal: The one who gave an experienced CPA all the relevant facts and took the recommended position.

items.topic: Taxpayer penalties
items.task: Identify taxpayer penalties given a specific scenario.
items.task_source: 지도.json
items.stem: The 2025 returns of the four taxpayers in the exhibit were due April 15, 2026. None has reasonable cause for any failure. Which taxpayer owes the failure-to-file addition to tax?
exhibit: $3,000 balance due, paid with the return
$6,000 balance due, paid with the return
No balance; estimated payments and withholding covered all of his tax
options: Nia
Petra
Omar
Quinn

why.A: Her return showed a refund, so no tax was unpaid on the due date. The addition is figured on the unpaid tax, so it is zero.
why.B: She had no extension and filed late with $3,000 of tax unpaid at the due date, so the failure-to-file addition applies to that unpaid tax.
why.C: His extension was timely and he filed within the extended due date, so he owes no failure-to-file addition. He may owe a failure-to-pay addition.
why.D: He filed late, but his payments covered all of his tax, so no tax was unpaid and the addition is zero.

items.law_note: A late return with no tax due after timely payments and credits produces no failure-to-file addition; the minimum penalty is not asked.
items.rule_line: The failure-to-file addition applies to tax unpaid at the original due date when the return is filed late without a valid extension.

guide.ask: When does the failure-to-file addition apply?
guide.reveal: On unpaid tax at the due date when the return is filed late without a valid extension.

guide.ask: Which of the four had no extension, a late return and tax unpaid at the due date?
guide.reveal: The taxpayer with no extension who filed July 20 with a $3,000 balance due; a refund, a valid extension or full prepayment leaves no unpaid tax.

items.topic: Taxpayer penalties
items.task: Identify taxpayer penalties given a specific scenario.
items.task_source: 지도.json
items.stem: Gordon Pell believes that wages are not income. He filed a signed 2024 return reporting zero income, and the return itself showed that its self-assessed tax was wrong. After the IRS issued a notice of deficiency, Gordon petitioned the Tax Court and repeated the same argument, which courts have rejected many times. Which penalty aimed at frivolous positions may apply to each action?
options: $5,000 for the return and up to $25,000 for the petition
$25,000 for the return and $5,000 for the petition
Nothing for the return, because a return reporting no income is not a return, and up to $25,000 for the petition
$5,000 for the return and nothing for the petition, because a Tax Court petition cannot be penalized

why.A: The IRS may assess a $5,000 penalty for a frivolous return, and the Tax Court may award up to $25,000 against a taxpayer whose position in the case is frivolous or groundless.
why.B: The amounts are reversed. $5,000 applies to the frivolous return and up to $25,000 to a frivolous Tax Court position.
why.C: The frivolous return penalty reaches a document that purports to be a return and shows on its face that the tax is wrong, so it applies to the return.
why.D: The Tax Court may award damages of up to $25,000 when a taxpayer's position is frivolous or groundless.

items.law_note: The $5,000 and $25,000 amounts are fixed statutory figures.
items.rule_line: The IRS may assess a $5,000 penalty on a frivolous return, and the Tax Court may award up to $25,000 for frivolous positions.

guide.ask: What penalty may the IRS assess on a frivolous return?
What may the Tax Court award against a frivolous or groundless position in a case?
guide.reveal: Up to $25,000, so both penalties may apply.

items.topic: Audits, appeals and the judicial process
items.task: Explain the audit and appeals process as it relates to tax matters.
items.task_source: 지도.json
items.stem: The IRS examined Ravi Kapoor's 2023 return and sent a 30-day letter proposing a $70,000 deficiency. Ravi did not respond and never filed a protest. The IRS then mailed a notice of deficiency, and Ravi filed a timely Tax Court petition. Which statement about Appeals is correct?
options: Ravi lost any chance at Appeals review when he ignored the 30-day letter, so the case can go only to trial
Appeals may consider a case only until a notice of deficiency is issued, so the petition ended its role in the case
Ravi can reach Appeals only by first paying the $70,000 and then filing a claim for refund with the IRS
Because Appeals has not yet considered the case, the IRS will generally refer the docketed case to Appeals for settlement talks

why.A: Ignoring the 30-day letter does not end Appeals review. Docketed cases are handled differently.
why.B: Appeals also handles docketed cases and can settle them after a petition is filed.
why.C: Appeals consideration does not require payment. Prepayment is a condition of a refund suit, not of Appeals.
why.D: Chief Counsel generally refers a docketed case to Appeals for settlement consideration unless Appeals itself issued the notice of deficiency, the taxpayer opts out, or an exception applies, such as a case designated for litigation. Appeals neither considered this case nor issued the notice, so referral is the general rule.

items.rule_line: A docketed Tax Court case is generally referred to Appeals for settlement even if the taxpayer never filed a protest.

guide.ask: Does ignoring the 30-day letter bar all Appeals review?
guide.reveal: No.

guide.ask: What happens to a docketed case Appeals has never considered?
guide.reveal: Chief Counsel generally refers it to Appeals for settlement, unless an exception such as designation for litigation applies.

items.topic: Legal duties and responsibilities
items.task: Identify the legal duties and responsibilities of tax practitioners (privilege, confidentiality, civil and criminal liability).
items.task_source: author-drafted from Blueprint topic name (지도.json has no Group A/B/D)
items.stem: Foster & Quill, CPAs, audited Tarn Holdings' financial statements. The firm knew that Tarn would give the audited statements to one or more banks to obtain a loan of about $2,000,000, but it did not know which banks and had no contact with any bank. The audit was negligent. Lakeview Bank lent Tarn $2,000,000 relying on the statements, and Ines Ward, who bought Tarn stock on the open market, also relied on them. Both lost money. Under which approach to accountants' liability to third parties could Lakeview recover for ordinary negligence, but Ines could not?
options: The Ultramares approach, which requires privity of contract with the auditor
The Credit Alliance approach, which requires a known user and conduct linking it to the auditor
The Restatement (Second) of Torts approach, which covers a limited group of intended users
The foreseeability approach, which covers users whose reliance the auditor could reasonably foresee

why.A: Neither Lakeview nor Ines had a contract with the auditor, so neither could recover for ordinary negligence.
why.B: The auditor did not know which banks would receive the statements and had no contact with any, so neither plaintiff meets the test.
why.C: Under Restatement Section 552 the auditor is liable to a limited group it knows will use the statements for a particular transaction. The banks Tarn would approach for the loan are such a group, but open-market stock buyers are not.
why.D: This approach reaches every foreseeable user, so Ines could recover along with Lakeview.

cite.ref: Credit Alliance Corp. v. Arthur Andersen & Co., 65 N.Y.2d 536 (1985)

items.rule_line: Under Restatement (Second) of Torts section 552, an auditor is liable to a known limited group of intended users, not open-market buyers.

guide.ask: Which approach protects a limited group of known intended users for a specific transaction?
guide.reveal: Restatement (Second) of Torts Section 552.

guide.ask: Which claimant fits that group and which does not?
guide.reveal: The bank the firm knew Tarn would approach for the loan fits; an open-market stock buyer does not.

items.topic: Legal duties and responsibilities
items.task: Identify the legal duties and responsibilities of tax practitioners (privilege, confidentiality, civil and criminal liability).
items.task_source: author-drafted from Blueprint topic name (지도.json has no Group A/B/D)
items.stem: A state follows the strict privity approach of Ultramares. Mira Voss, CPA, issued an unmodified opinion on Corvane Inc.'s financial statements without confirming any accounts receivable or inspecting inventory, even though her own workpapers flagged large unexplained sales. The statements later proved materially false. Corvane's lender, which had no contract with Mira and was unknown to her, sued for its loss. Which statement is correct?
options: The lender cannot recover on any theory, because it had no contract with Mira and she did not know it
The lender may recover if it proves that Mira was grossly negligent or reckless, which counts as constructive fraud
The lender may recover only if Mira knew who the lender was when she issued the unmodified opinion
The lender may recover on a showing of ordinary negligence, because its loss from the false statements was foreseeable

why.A: Privity is not required when the auditor's conduct is fraudulent, and reckless disregard of obvious warning signs can be treated as constructive fraud.
why.B: Under Ultramares, gross negligence so serious that it implies fraud can support liability to a third party who relied, even without privity.
why.C: Knowing the identity of the user matters for negligence claims under other approaches, not for liability based on fraud or constructive fraud.
why.D: Foreseeability supports ordinary negligence liability only in states that follow the foreseeability approach. This state follows strict privity.

items.rule_line: Under Ultramares, a third party may recover without privity if the auditor's gross negligence or recklessness amounts to constructive fraud.

guide.ask: Does privity matter under Ultramares for ordinary negligence?
guide.reveal: Yes, ordinary negligence needs privity.

guide.ask: What conduct supports liability to a third party without privity?
guide.reveal: Gross negligence so serious it implies fraud, and Mira's unmodified opinion with no confirmations despite flagged sales meets that standard.

items.topic: Legal duties and responsibilities
items.task: Identify the legal duties and responsibilities of tax practitioners (privilege, confidentiality, civil and criminal liability).
items.task_source: author-drafted from Blueprint topic name (지도.json has no Group A/B/D)
items.stem: Two investors sue an auditor over the same materially misstated financial statements. Ada bought shares in a registered public offering and sues under the Securities Act of 1933 provision that makes experts liable for misstatements in a registration statement. Ben bought shares on the open market and sues under the general antifraud provisions of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934. Which of the following must Ben prove that Ada need not prove?
options: That the auditor acted with intent to deceive or reckless disregard and that Ben relied on the report
That the audited financial statements contained a material misstatement or omission when the shares were sold
That Ben suffered a monetary loss on the shares he bought after the statements were issued
That the auditor had a contract with Ben or knew who he was when it issued the audit report

why.A: The antifraud claim requires scienter and reliance. The registration statement claim generally requires neither.
why.B: Ada must also prove a material misstatement in the registration statement, so this is not an added burden for Ben.
why.C: Both plaintiffs must show damages, so this is not an added burden for Ben.
why.D: Neither claim requires privity of contract or knowledge of the plaintiff's identity.

items.rule_line: A 1934 Act antifraud claim requires scienter and reliance, unlike a 1933 Act registration statement claim.

guide.ask: What does a 1934 Act antifraud claim require beyond a material misstatement?
guide.reveal: Scienter, meaning intent to deceive or reckless disregard, and reliance.

guide.ask: Does a 1933 Act registration statement claim require those?
guide.reveal: Generally not, so those are the extra items Ben must prove.

items.topic: Legal duties and responsibilities
items.task: Identify the legal duties and responsibilities of tax practitioners (privilege, confidentiality, civil and criminal liability).
items.task_source: author-drafted from Blueprint topic name (지도.json has no Group A/B/D)
items.stem: Purchasers in a public offering sue the company's auditors under the Securities Act of 1933, alleging a material misstatement in the audited financial statements included in the registration statement. Which of the following is a valid defense for the auditors?
options: The purchasers did not read or rely on the audited statements when they bought their shares in the offering
The auditors had no contract with the purchasers and had no contact with them before the offering
The auditors did not intend to deceive anyone and believed in good faith that the statements were fairly presented
The auditors made a reasonable investigation and reasonably believed the statements were true when the registration became effective

why.A: Reliance is generally not an element of the registration statement claim, so lack of reliance is not a defense.
why.B: Privity is not required for the registration statement claim.
why.C: Intent is not an element, and a good-faith belief without a reasonable investigation does not meet the due diligence defense.
why.D: This is the due diligence defense for experts. The auditors must show a reasonable investigation and a reasonable ground to believe, and actual belief, that the statements were true.

items.rule_line: An expert's due diligence defense under the 1933 Act requires a reasonable investigation and reasonable belief that the statements were true.

guide.ask: What defense do auditors have in a 1933 Act suit over a registration statement?
guide.reveal: Due diligence.

guide.ask: What must they show?
guide.reveal: A reasonable investigation and reasonable ground to believe, and actual belief, that the statements were true when the registration became effective.

items.topic: Legal duties and responsibilities
items.task: Identify the legal duties and responsibilities of tax practitioners (privilege, confidentiality, civil and criminal liability).
items.task_source: author-drafted from Blueprint topic name (지도.json has no Group A/B/D)
items.stem: Delphine Ross, CPA, gave her client Arclight Corp. a memorandum of tax advice about a proposed reorganization. The memorandum is protected by the federally authorized tax practitioner privilege in a civil tax matter. Which later event most likely waives the privilege for the memorandum?
options: Arclight's chief financial officer, who needs the advice to carry out the plan, shares the memorandum with two finance managers
Arclight gives a copy of the memorandum to its outside lender to help win approval of a related loan
Delphine discusses the memorandum with a partner in her firm who is helping on the engagement
The IRS opens an examination of Arclight's return and asks about the reorganization

why.A: Sharing within the client on a need-to-know basis does not waive the privilege.
why.B: Voluntary disclosure of privileged advice to an outsider such as a lender waives the privilege for that communication.
why.C: Consulting within the practitioner's own firm on the engagement does not waive the privilege.
why.D: An IRS examination or request for information does not waive the privilege. Only the client's voluntary disclosure does.

items.rule_line: Voluntary disclosure of privileged tax advice to an outsider such as a lender waives the tax practitioner privilege.

guide.ask: What waives the tax practitioner privilege?
guide.reveal: Voluntary disclosure of the privileged advice to an outsider.

guide.ask: Which event discloses the memorandum outside the company and its advisers?
guide.reveal: Handing a copy to the outside lender; internal sharing and IRS inquiries do not waive.

items.topic: Legal duties and responsibilities
items.task: Identify the legal duties and responsibilities of tax practitioners (privilege, confidentiality, civil and criminal liability).
items.task_source: author-drafted from Blueprint topic name (지도.json has no Group A/B/D)
items.stem: Reese Duran, a paid return preparer, knowingly listed fictitious business expenses on a client's return to increase the client's refund. The client, Alma, believed the return was accurate, did not know about the expenses, and signed it. Which statement about Reese's criminal exposure is correct?
options: He may be convicted of willfully assisting in a false return, even though Alma did not know it was false
He cannot be convicted, because Alma signed the return herself and had no intent to defraud anyone
He may be convicted only if the IRS also proves that Alma is liable for the civil fraud penalty on the return
He faces at most a misdemeanor, because preparers are not subject to the felony provisions of the tax code

why.A: The statute reaches anyone who willfully aids or assists in preparing a false return, whether or not the taxpayer knows of the falsity.
why.B: The taxpayer's signature and innocence do not protect a preparer who willfully assists in a false return.
why.C: No finding of civil fraud against the client is required for the preparer's conviction.
why.D: Willfully assisting in a false return is a felony that applies to preparers.

items.rule_line: A preparer who willfully assists in preparing a false return commits a felony even if the taxpayer is unaware of the falsity.

guide.ask: What does the criminal aiding statute cover?
guide.reveal: Anyone who willfully aids or assists in preparing a false return.

guide.ask: Does it matter that the client was unaware and signed?
guide.reveal: No, the taxpayer's knowledge is not required, so Reese may be convicted.

items.topic: Legal duties and responsibilities
items.task: Identify the legal duties and responsibilities of tax practitioners (privilege, confidentiality, civil and criminal liability).
items.task_source: author-drafted from Blueprint topic name (지도.json has no Group A/B/D)
items.stem: In a private class action under the antifraud provisions of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934, a jury finds that Larkin & Shaw, the company's auditor, is 30% responsible for the investors' loss because it acted recklessly but not knowingly. The company's officers, who acted knowingly, are found 70% responsible. How is Larkin & Shaw's liability for damages determined?
options: Jointly and severally liable for all of the damages, because any auditor found liable under the antifraud provisions is jointly and severally liable
Not liable at all, because an auditor is liable under the antifraud provisions only if it knew the statements were false
Generally liable only for its own percentage of responsibility, because reckless conduct is not treated as a knowing violation
Jointly and severally liable, because the case was certified as a class action

why.A: Joint and several liability applies only to a defendant that knowingly committed the violation, not to every auditor found liable.
why.B: Recklessness satisfies the scienter requirement in most courts, so actual knowledge is not needed for liability.
why.C: Under the Private Securities Litigation Reform Act, joint and several liability requires a knowing violation. Reckless conduct is not treated as knowing, so liability is generally proportionate.
why.D: Class certification does not change the liability rule.

cite.ref: Private Securities Litigation Reform Act of 1995

items.rule_line: Under the PSLRA, joint and several liability requires a knowing violation, so reckless defendants are liable only proportionately.

guide.ask: What does joint and several liability require under the Private Securities Litigation Reform Act?
guide.reveal: A knowing violation.

guide.ask: Was the auditor's conduct knowing or reckless, and what follows?
guide.reveal: Reckless, so liability is generally limited to its own 30% share.
